subject: phy
title: Atoms and Nuclei
syllabus: Alpha-particle scattering experiment; Rutherford's model of atom; Bohr model, energy levels, hydrogen spectrum. Composition and size of nucleus, atomic masses, mass-energy relation, mass defect; binding energy per nucleon and its variation with mass number, nuclear fission and fusion.

body: Most α-particles pass straight through gold foil; a very few bounce back → all the positive charge and almost all the mass sit in a tiny nucleus.
closest approach: K = \f{k(2e)(Ze)}{r_{0}}
Only particles with a tiny impact parameter (nearly head-on) are thrown back. Thomson's "plum pudding" could not explain this.

check.q: Doubling the α energy makes the closest approach :

body: KE = −E, PE = 2E (so E = \f{PE}{2}). f ∝ \f{Z^{2}}{n^{3}}; magnetic moment ∝ n; field at the nucleus ∝ \f{1}{n^{5}}.
Works only for one-electron atoms (H, He^{+}, Li^{2+}) — it ignores electron–electron repulsion.
Same energy for two ions when \f{Z}{n} is the same.

body: Lyman (→1, UV), Balmer (→2, visible), Paschen (→3, IR). Longest λ = first line; shortest = series limit (n_{2} → ∞).
From level n, many atoms give \f{n(n − 1)}{2} lines.
To see any Balmer line from the ground state, give at least 12.09 eV (reach n = 3). An emitting atom recoils with p = \f{E}{c}.

check.q: Shortest Balmer λ : shortest Lyman λ =

body: R = R_{0}A^{1/3} (R_{0} ≈ 1.2 fm), Δm = Zm_{p} + (A − Z)m_{n} − M, BE = Δm × 931.5 MeV
Nuclear density is the same for all nuclei (~2.3 × 10^{17} kg/m^{3}).
BE/A is about 8 MeV for 30 < A < 170, peaks near Fe-56, and is low for very light and very heavy nuclei. Nuclear force: strong, short-range, charge-independent.
Isotopes: same Z · isobars: same A · isotones: same N.

check.q: A nucleus with 8 times the mass number has radius :

body: Q = Σ BE(products) − Σ BE(reactants) = (mass before − mass after) × 931.5 MeV
Heavy nuclei split (fission, ~200 MeV per U-235) and light ones join (fusion, e.g. 2 ^{2}H → ^{4}He) — both move towards higher BE/A.
Balance A and Z in every reaction (neutrons: A = 1, Z = 0). In a two-body break-up from rest, momenta are equal and opposite: K ∝ \f{1}{m}; α gets Q\f{A − 4}{A}.
Beta decay: n → p + e^{−} + ν̄.

check.q: Fission of A = 236 (7.6 MeV/nucleon) into two A = 118 (8.5 MeV/nucleon) releases :

body: After n half-lives, \f{1}{2^{n}} remains. Activity falls the same way.
Chain P → Q → R (stable): P falls, Q rises to a peak and falls, R keeps growing.

check.q: After 3 half-lives the fraction left is :

traps: Longest wavelength of a series = its FIRST line; shortest = its limit.
L is a multiple of h/2π, not of h.
Nuclear density does not depend on A.
Neutrino goes with e⁺, antineutrino with e⁻.
Many atoms in level n: n(n − 1)/2 lines; ONE atom: at most n − 1.

steps.note: Size, binding energy, fission, fusion and decay

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A : The Bohr model is applicable to hydrogen and hydrogen-like atoms only. Reason R : The formulation of Bohr model does not include repulsive force between electrons. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
sol: Bohr's model has one electron in the Coulomb field of the nucleus — it cannot handle electron–electron repulsion.
So it works only for one-electron (hydrogen-like) systems: both true, R explains A.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

Statement (II) : In Bohr's model electron revolve around the nucleus only in those orbits for which angular momentum is integral multiple of Planck's constant. sol: The dip at 10.2 V means atoms absorb 10.2 eV (n = 1 → 2).

pyq.q: In a hypothetical fission reaction ^{236}_{92}X → ^{141}_{56}Y + ^{92}_{36}Z + 3R. The identity of emitted particles (R) is :
sol: Each R carries A = \f{236 − 233}{3} = 1 and Z = 0 → neutron.

pyq.q: Match the LIST-I with LIST-II. LIST-I: A. ^{1}_{0}n + ^{235}_{92}U → ^{140}_{54}Xe + ^{94}_{38}Sr + 2^{1}_{0}n B. H_{2} + O_{2} → 2H_{2}O C. ^{2}_{1}H + ^{2}_{1}H → ^{3}_{2}He + ^{1}_{0}n D. ^{1}_{1}H + ^{3}_{1}H → ^{2}_{1}H + ^{2}_{1}H. LIST-II: I. Chemical reaction II. Fusion with +ve Q value III. Fission IV. Fusion with −ve Q value. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
sol: A: U splits → fission. B: no nuclei change → chemical.
C: D + D → He-3 releases ≈ 3.3 MeV (+Q fusion).
D: ^{1}H + ^{3}H → 2 ^{2}H needs energy (BE: 8.48 before vs 2 × 2.22 after) → −Q.

pyq.q: Choose the correct nuclear process from the below options [p : proton, n : neutron, e^{−} : electron, e^{+} : positron, ν : neutrino, ν̄ : antineutrino]
sol: Charge: 0 = +1 − 1 → an electron must come out.
Lepton number: 0 = 0 + 1 − 1 → with an electron goes an ANTI-neutrino.

pyq.q: In a nuclear fission reaction of an isotope of mass M, three similar daughter nuclei of same mass are formed. The speed of a daughter nuclei in terms of mass defect ΔM will be :
sol: Energy ΔMc^{2} → KE of three pieces of mass \f{M}{3} each (equal speeds by symmetry).

pyq.q: A nucleus at rest disintegrates into two smaller nuclei with their masses in the ratio of 2 : 1. After disintegration they will move :-
sol: Momentum conservation: 2m v_{1} = m v_{2} → v_{1} : v_{2} = 1 : 2, opposite directions.
o: In opposite directions with speed in the ratio of 1:2 respectively
In opposite directions with speed in the ratio of 2:1 respectively
In the same direction with same speed.
In opposite directions with the same speed.

pyq.q: The minimum frequency of photon required to break a particle of mass 15.348 amu into 4α particles is ______ kHz. [mass of He nucleus = 4.002 amu, 1 amu = 1.66 × 10^{−27} kg, h = 6.6 × 10^{−34} J s and c = 3 × 10^{8} m/s]
Two radioactive substances A and B of mass numbers 200 and 212 respectively, shows spontaneous α-decay with same Q value of 1 MeV. The ratio of energies of α-rays produced by A and B is____
sol: Momentum shared equally → α gets Q × \f{A − 4}{A}.

pyq.q: A radioactive nucleus n_{2} has 3 times the decay constant as compared to the decay constant of another radioactive nucleus n_{1}. If initial number of both nuclei are the same, what is the ratio of number of nuclei of n_{2} to the number of nuclei of n_{1}, after one half-life of n_{1}?
A radioactive material P first decays into Q and then Q decays to non-radioactive material R. Which of the following figure represents time dependent mass of P, Q and R ?
sol: Q is made from P and decays itself: starts at 0, rises, peaks, then falls.
R only grows, approaching the starting amount of P.
o: P falls, Q rises steadily and levels off at the top, R rises late
P and R rise and fall together, Q rises steadily
P falls from its start, Q rises to a peak and then falls, R rises from zero towards the total
P falls, Q and R both rise and level off

pyq.q: In an alpha particle scattering experiment distance of closest approach for the α particle is 4.5 × 10^{−14} m. If target nucleus has atomic number 80, then maximum velocity of α-particle is ______ × 10^{5} m/s approximately. (\f{1}{4πε_{0}} = 9 × 10^{9} SI unit, mass of α particle = 6.72 × 10^{−27} kg)

If an alpha particle with energy 7.7 MeV is bombarded on a thin gold foil, the closest distance from nucleus it can reach is _____ m. (Atomic number of gold = 79 and \f{1}{4πε_{0}} = 9 × 10^{9} in SI units)

7.9 MeV α-particle scatters from a target material of atomic number 79. From the given data the estimated diameter of nuclei of the target material is (approximately)_____ m. [\f{1}{4πε_{0}} = 9 × 10^{9} N m^{2}/C^{2} and electron charge = 1.6 × 10^{−19} C]
sol: Closest approach (head-on) estimates the nuclear radius: r_{0} = \f{9 × 10^{9} × 158 × 1.6 × 10^{−19}}{7.9 × 10^{6}} ≈ 2.88 × 10^{−14} m.

pyq.q: In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, only a few alpha particles rebound back because A. The size of gold nucleus is very small as compared to the size of gold atom. B. Alpha particle and gold nucleus have equal charge. C. The impact parameter is minimum for a few alpha particles. D. A few alpha particles have very high kinetic energy. E. Only a few alpha particles undergo head-on collision with the nuclei. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
sol: A tiny nucleus (A) means only a few α come with near-zero impact parameter (C), i.e. nearly head-on (E).
B is false (2e vs 79e); D is not the reason (all have the same energy).
